title: Applications of storage
starter: Pick three devices in the room and say what kind of storage each one uses, and why that suits it.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: How to choose
facts: Ask: how much data? How fast? Does it need carrying? How long must it last? What's the budget?
Then match those answers to a device's characteristics.
stations.challenge: What questions would you ask a customer before recommending storage?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Ask: how much data? How fast? Does it need carrying? How long must it last? What's the budget?
Also credit: Then match those answers to a device's characteristics.

questions.q: Which question matters most for choosing storage for a video camera?
questions.a: How portable and durable does it need to be?

questions.q: A customer needs 12 TB for a backup server on a tight budget. What matters most?

stations.name: Distributing a film
facts: Millions of copies, posted or sold in shops.
Each copy must be cheap, light and hold a couple of hours of high-definition video.
Read-only is fine: buyers don't need to write to it.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Millions of copies, posted or sold in shops.
Also credit: Each copy must be cheap, light and hold a couple of hours of high-definition video.

questions.q: Which storage is most suitable for selling a film in shops?
questions.a: Optical disc, such as Blu-ray: cheap to mass produce and easy to post

questions.q: Why is read-only acceptable for this?
questions.a: Customers only need to watch the film, not write to the disc

stations.name: Carrying work home
facts: Small files, carried in a pocket every day.
Needs to survive knocks and plug into any computer.
Capacity needed is small compared with a server.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Small files, carried in a pocket every day.
Also credit: Needs to survive knocks and plug into any computer.

questions.q: Which device suits carrying work between home and an office?
questions.a: A USB flash drive: small, portable and durable

questions.q: Which characteristic is least important here?

stations.name: Music, cameras and consoles
facts: MP3 player: small, no moving parts, survives movement, so solid state.
Video camera: fast writes and portability, so a solid state memory card.
Console game: mass-produced, so optical disc, or a download.
stations.challenge: Which device for each, and why?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: MP3 player: small, no moving parts, survives movement, so solid state.
Also credit: Video camera: fast writes and portability, so a solid state memory card.

questions.q: Match each situation to the most suitable storage.
questions.a: MP3 player → Solid state: small, light, survives movement; Video camera → Solid state memory card: fast writes and portable; Console game in a shop → Optical disc: cheap to mass produce; School network main storage → Magnetic hard disks: large capacity at low cost

stations.name: Servers and operating systems
facts: School network storage: many terabytes, always plugged in, so magnetic hard disks.
A computer's operating system: needs to load fast, so solid state.
Servers often use both: SSD for speed, hard disks for bulk.
stations.challenge: Why do servers often use two types of storage together?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: School network storage: many terabytes, always plugged in, so magnetic hard disks.
Also credit: A computer's operating system: needs to load fast, so solid state.

questions.q: Why do schools use magnetic hard disks for bulk network storage?
questions.a: They give the most gigabytes for the money and never leave the server room

questions.q: Why is an SSD used for a computer's operating system?
questions.a: It loads and responds much faster than a hard disk

stations.name: Long-term archives
facts: Training videos kept for years: huge capacity, rarely accessed, so magnetic tape or archive discs.
Photo backups: a second copy, kept somewhere else, often an external hard disk or the cloud.
Any backup should be kept away from the original.
stations.challenge: Which device for long-term photo backup, and why?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Training videos kept for years: huge capacity, rarely accessed, so magnetic tape or archive discs.
Also credit: Photo backups: a second copy, kept somewhere else, often an external hard disk or the cloud.

questions.q: A company archives 200 TB of training videos it rarely opens. Which is most suitable?
questions.a: Magnetic tape: enormous capacity at the lowest cost

questions.q: Why should a photo backup be kept in a different place from the originals?
questions.a: A fire, flood or theft could destroy both copies at once

final.name: Final challenge: nine customers

questions.q: Which type of storage is most suitable for each situation?
questions.a: Distributing a film to shops = Optical; Transferring work between home and an office = Solid state; Storing tracks on an MP3 player = Solid state; Main storage for a school network = Magnetic; Storing video on a video camera = Solid state; Distributing a video game for a console = Optical; Storing a computer's operating system = Solid state; Long-term storage of training videos = Magnetic; Long-term backup of photos = Magnetic

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: A photographer needs storage for use on location. Recommend a device and justify your choice.
points: Needs to survive knocks and plug into any computer.
A computer's operating system: needs to load fast, so solid state.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

exam.q: Explain why a school uses magnetic hard disks rather than SSDs for its main file storage.
points: School network storage: many terabytes, always plugged in, so magnetic hard disks.
Servers often use both: SSD for speed, hard disks for bulk.
Training videos kept for years: huge capacity, rarely accessed, so magnetic tape or archive discs.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
